Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 26, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

## Psalm 26 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Background and Setting

**Title / Occasion.** Spurgeon notes the psalm presents David "as one enduring reproach … the type of the great Son of David." He mentions "an ingenious surmise that this appeal to heaven was written by David at the time of the assassination of Ishbosheth, by Baanah and Rechab, to protest his innocence of all participation in that treacherous murder." The tenor of the psalm fits, but Spurgeon cautions the clue is too slender for certainty. Gill likewise ties it to David's quarrel with Saul — "the former listening to calumnies and reproaches cast upon the latter, and persecuting him in a violent manner." He notes Theodoret thought it was written when David fled from Saul.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm (via search excerpt)

**Relation to Psalm 25.** Christopher Wordsworth (quoted by Spurgeon) says Psalm 26 "is coupled on to the foregoing by thoughts and words." Psalm 25 closes with a prayer for integrity (v.21); Psalm 26 picks up that theme. Wordsworth adds: "Unless this Psalm is regarded as a sequel to the preceding one, it will seem vainglorious; but being combined with the penitential acknowledgments of sin … it will be seen that the declarations which the psalmist now makes of integrity, are not assertions of human merit, but acknowledgments of divine mercy." Augustine is quoted: *"Non merita mea, sed misericordia tua, ante oculos meos est"* — "Not my merits, but your mercy, is before my eyes."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

**Structure (David Dickson, cited by Spurgeon):** vv.1–3 — appeal to God based on upright walk as a believer; vv.4–5 — separation from the contagion of the wicked; vv.6–8 — purpose to behave holily out of love for the public privileges of God's people; vv.9–10 — prayer to be spared the judgment coming on the wicked; v.11 — resolution to eschew their sins; v.12 — closes with comfort and assurance of being heard.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

---

### Verse 1

**"Vindicate me, O LORD! For I have walked with integrity; I have trusted in the LORD without wavering."**

**Traditional Reading.** David makes a solemn appeal to God as Judge. Spurgeon writes: "Worried and worn out by the injustice of men, the innocent spirit flies from its false accusers to the throne of Eternal Right." He warns, however, that "such an appeal as this is not to be rashly made on any occasion; and as to the whole of our walk and conversation, it should never be made at all, except as we are justified in Christ Jesus." David Guzik (Enduring Word) says "David's vindication is less about his reputation with people and more about God's reputation — he wanted God's name honored, not his own." The BSB's "without wavering" is rendered by older translations as "I shall not slide." Spurgeon explains: "Slippery as the way is, so that I walk like a man upon ice, yet faith keeps my heels from tripping." Barton Bouchier (in Spurgeon) notes: "It is not … 'I shall not fall,' but … 'I shall not even slide;' not even make a false step or stumble."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

**"Integrity."** Gill explains that David means "the purity of his intentions and designs; the uprightness of his conduct, the simplicity and sincerity of his conduct towards all men, and especially his fidelity to his prince." He is not claiming sinlessness — "not that he thought himself free from sin; this would be contrary to the complaints, confessions, and petitions frequently made by him." Rather, in the specific affair with Saul he was innocent (1 Sam 24:9). Spurgeon says: "He held integrity as his principle, and walked in it as his practice. David had not used any traitorous or unrighteous means to gain the crown, or to keep it."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm

**Faith as root of integrity.** Spurgeon: "Faith is the root and sap of integrity. He who leans upon the Lord is sure to walk in righteousness." Hengstenberg (quoted by Spurgeon): "Trust in God is the fountain of 'integrity.' Whoever places his hope in God need not seek to advance his worldly interests by violating his duty towards his neighbour."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

**Piper (Reformed Baptist).** John Piper uses Psalm 26:1 to address the broader question of the psalmists' claims of blamelessness: "This is not pride. This is not self-reliance. This is not legalism. This is not salvation-by-works. This is a godly man, trusting the mercy of God, knowing his sins are forgiven, walking in the power of God's sanctifying Spirit." He argues that imputed righteousness is the foundation but not the summation — "The faith that unites us to Christ for justification also leads to sanctification."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/can-anyone-really-be-blameless

---

### Verse 2

**"Test me, O LORD, and try me; examine my heart and mind."**

**Traditional Reading.** David submits unconditionally to divine examination. Spurgeon notes the three verbs correspond to "trial by touch, trial by smell, and trial by fire" in the original. Albert Barnes (in Spurgeon): "These words are designed to include all the modes in which the reality of anything is tested; and they imply together that he wished the most thorough investigation to be made; he did not shrink from any test." Guzik: "The request to examine, prove, and try refers mainly to the inward working of a man or woman — the mind and the heart." Ellicott notes the LXX renders "try" as "purify" — "try by fire."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm

**"Heart and mind" (reins and heart).** The Hebrew refers to the kidneys (seat of affections) and the heart (seat of thought and will). Gill: "the thoughts, desires, and affections of it, as gold and silver are tried in the furnace." Robert Cawdray (in Spurgeon): "As gold, by fire, is severed and parted from dross, so singleness of heart and true Christian simplicity is best seen and made most evident in troubles and afflictions."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

**Wiersbe (Precept Austin).** Wiersbe sees this as "Step 1: An honest examination." He comments: "Human nature does not want to admit it's wrong, but we need to examine ourselves. … We find David open before God, walking in the light and letting God examine him. We would save ourselves a lot of trouble if we would let Him examine us."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/Integrity_a_whole_heart

---

### Verse 3

**"For Your loving devotion is before my eyes, and I have walked in Your truth."**

**Traditional Reading.** God's *chesed* (lovingkindness / loving devotion) is the motive for David's walk. Spurgeon waxes long: "Dwell, dear reader, upon that celestial word lovingkindness. It has a heavenly savour. Is it not an unmatchable word, unexcelled, unrivalled?" He adds: "Men sin with the law before their eyes, but divine love, when clearly seen, sanctifies the conversation." Guzik quotes Spurgeon's sermon outline on the lovingkindness of God: "His lovingkindness begins in eternity … is given freely … is certain … is faithful … goes into the smallest details." Gill says this lovingkindness refers to "the special lovingkindness of God, shown in the choice of him in Christ, in the provision of a Saviour for him, and in the effectual calling of him." It is "before his eyes" means "he had a comfortable view of interest in it, and was persuaded nothing should separate him from it."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm

**"Walked in Your truth."** Ellicott says God's truth "formed the rule of his life." Gill says this means walking "by faith in Christ, who is the truth of all promises, prophecies, types, and figures; in the word of truth … and in the truth of worship, in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord." Guzik adds: "The idea of walked speaks of action, of manner of living. David knew the importance of both a right inward life (mind and heart) and right actions and deeds."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

---

### Verse 4

**"I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites."**

**Traditional Reading.** David lists specific evidence of a faithful life: separation from evil associates. The BSB's "deceitful men" is rendered by older versions as "vain persons" or "idolatrous mortals." Spurgeon: "True citizens have no dealings with traitors. David had no seat in the parliament of triflers. … Not only the profane, but the vain are to be shunned by us. All those who live for this life only are vain, chaffy, frothy men, quite unworthy of a Christian's friendship." Gill explains "vain persons … who are full of vanity; who are addicted to the vanities of the world … whose thoughts, words, and actions are vain." Poole (quoted by Guzik): "I have not sat, i.e. chosen or used to converse with them; for sitting is a posture of ease and continuance." Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik) says "hypocrites" are "the hidden ones, the dark designers, the secret plotters."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

**Wiersbe (Precept Austin).** This is "Step 2: A holy separation." Wiersbe writes: "People accused David of being a hypocrite, even though he did not worship false gods. We must obey the biblical doctrine of holy separation (2Cor. 6:14–18)."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/Integrity_a_whole_heart

---

### Verse 5

**"I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked."**

**Traditional Reading.** The separation is not merely passive avoidance; it includes a moral revulsion. Spurgeon: "A man who does not hate evil terribly, does not love good heartily. Men, as men, we must always love … but evil doers, as such, are traitors to the Great King, and no loyal subject can love traitors. What God hates we must hate." He notes the grim parallel: "What a sad reflection it is that there should be a congregation of evil doers as well as a congregation of the upright, a church of Satan as well as a church of God." The BSB's "mob" translates "congregation/assembly" — Ellicott says "evil doers" carries "idea of violence; from a root meaning to break in pieces." Gill says David hated "their works and actions … though not their persons; and showed his displicency at them, and dislike and disapprobation of them, by absenting from them."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/26.htm

---

### Verse 6

**"I wash my hands in innocence that I may go about Your altar, O LORD."**

**Traditional Reading.** A symbolic action declaring innocence (cf. Deut. 21:6; Matt. 27:24), followed by worship at the altar. Ellicott says the hand-washing is "first a symbolical action … then a figure of speech (Job 9:30; Ezekiel 36:25)." He notes that "the Levitical authorship or, at all events, the Levitical character of the psalm appears from comparison of this with Exodus 30:17 seq." Regarding "go about / compass Your altar," Ellicott observes: "There is no other reference in Jewish literature to the custom of pacing round the altar, but it was a very natural and obvious addition to a gorgeous ceremonial — like the processions in churches where a high ceremonial is adopted. It is, however, implied from the Talmud that it was part of the ceremonial of the Feast of Tabernacles for people to march round the altar with palms." Guzik notes Poole's alternative: "He implies that he would offer many sacrifices together, which would employ the priests about the altar." Spurgeon: "Priests unto God must take great care to be personally cleansed; the brazen laver was as needful as the golden altar."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

**Guzik adds:** "David did not believe he was sinless or perfect. He did need to wash his hands, but he could do so in the innocence of a clear conscience before God. He availed himself of God's altar, both for atonement and for offerings of thanksgiving."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

**Wiersbe (Precept Austin):** "Step 3: A happy celebration. David washed his hands in innocence. He was cleansed by water and blood. He was concerned about praising, loving and glorifying God. Just as Jesus sang before His crucifixion, David sang songs of praise around the altar, the place of sacrifice."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/Integrity_a_whole_heart

---

### Verse 7

**"to raise my voice in thanksgiving and declare all Your wonderful works."**

**Traditional Reading.** The purpose of approaching the altar is public praise. Spurgeon: "David was so far instructed that he does not mention the typical offering, but discerns the spiritual offering which was intended thereby — not the groans of bullocks, but songs of gratitude the spiritual worshipper presents." He adds: "Let men slander us as they will, let us not defraud the Lord of his praises; let dogs bark, but let us like the moon shine on." Ellicott: "Literally, to make to hear the voice of praise."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm

---

### Verse 8

**"O LORD, I love the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides."**

**Traditional Reading.** David expresses deep affection for the tabernacle, the place of God's manifest presence. Spurgeon: "Into the abodes of sin he would not enter, but the house of God he had long loved, and loved it still. We were sad children if we did not love our Father's dwelling place." Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik) identifies "the habitation" as "the holy of holies, where the Divine Presence was manifest; and the place of the tabernacle must refer to the mercy-seat, or the place where the glory of the Lord appeared between the cherubim, upon the lid or cover of the ark of the covenant." Guzik: "For David, a right walk with God was more than the avoidance of evil. It was also a simple yet deep love for God and His presence. … Obedience cannot be sustained without the sweetness of God's presence and glory." Utley notes this imagery originally referred to the wilderness tabernacle (Exodus 25–31; 36–40) but later to the Jerusalem temple, and that "faithful followers longed to be in YHWH's presence (cf. Psalms 23:6; 27:4–5)."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/psalms-26.html

---

### Verse 9

**"Do not take my soul away with sinners, or my life with men of bloodshed."**

**Traditional Reading.** David prays to be spared when judgment falls on the wicked. Spurgeon: "Lord, when, like fruit, I must be gathered, put me not in the same basket with the best of sinners, much less with the worst of them. The company of sinners is so distasteful to us here, that we cannot endure the thought of being bound up in the same bundle with them to all eternity." He adds: "Our comfort is, that the Great Husbandman discerns the tares from the wheat, and will find a separate place for distinct characters." Guzik: "He refused to associate with the wicked in life; he asked God to keep him from sinners in death." Ellicott says the margin reading "Gather not" is better than "take … away," and explains: "The psalmist prays that he may be spared to worship in the sanctuary, when doom falls on evildoers and carries them off." The LXX and Vulgate have "destroy not."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm

**Spurgeon also quotes himself:** "The worst and most abandoned wretch on earth agrees with David in this. Sinners do not wish to be gathered with sinners. Balaam's prayer is, 'Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his,' which only differs in words from David's petition, 'Gather not my soul with sinners.'"
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

---

### Verse 10

**"in whose hands are wicked schemes, whose right hands are full of bribes."**

**Traditional Reading.** The character of the wicked is exposed: scheming and bribery. Spurgeon: "They have both hands full of it, plotting it and carrying it out. And their right hand, with which they are most dexterous, is full of bribes; like thieves who would steal with impunity, they carry a sop for the dogs of justice." He adds: "He who gives bribes is every way as guilty as the man who takes them." Guzik applies it broadly: "Many who would never think of taking bribes from a businessman still take bribes of a sort; they take bribes from sin. A bribe simply is a reward for doing something morally wrong." William Gurnall (quoted by Spurgeon): "A soul walking in its integrity will take bribes neither from men, nor sin itself."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

---

### Verse 11

**"But I will walk with integrity; redeem me and be merciful to me."**

**Traditional Reading.** A resolution paired with dependence. Guzik: "David had appropriate resolve, but even more appropriate trust in God. He could only walk in integrity if God would redeem him and be merciful to him." Spurgeon: "Here is the lover of godliness entering his personal protest against unrighteous gain. He is a Nonconformist, and is ready to stand alone in his Nonconformity. Like a live fish, he swims against the stream." Yet Spurgeon warns against self-righteousness: "Our integrity is not absolute nor inherent, it is a work of grace in us, and is marred by human infirmity; we must, therefore, resort to the redeeming blood and to the throne of mercy, confessing that though we are saints among men, we must still bow as sinners before God."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

**Wiersbe (Precept Austin):** "Step 4: A humble determination. David said, 'As for me, I will walk in my integrity.' When a person has integrity, he has a great defense, a great shield. Character is a marvelous shield against the accusations of men. A good conscience gives us courage in times of difficulty."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/Integrity_a_whole_heart

---

### Verse 12

**"My feet stand on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the LORD."**

**Traditional Reading.** The psalm closes on a note of confident praise. Guzik notes that "my foot stands in an even place" circles back to "I shall not slip" in v.1 — an inclusio. Spurgeon: "The song began in the minor, but it has now reached the major key. Saints often sing themselves into happiness. The even place upon which our foot stands is the sure, covenant faithfulness, eternal promise and immutable oath of the Lord of Hosts; there is no fear of falling from this solid basis, or of its being removed from under us." He adds: "Established in Christ Jesus, by being vitally united to him, we have nothing left to occupy our thoughts but the praises of our God." Guzik: "He was so confident that he said that he would bless and praise God publicly, among others (in the congregations), not as an outcast or castaway." Ellicott suggests the sense is: "When I stand in an even or level place [i.e., when I am rescued from the difficulties which now beset me] I will praise Jehovah in the congregation."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm

---

## Denominational Perspectives

### Reformed / Reformed Baptist — John Piper (Desiring God)

The key theological tension in Psalm 26 is how to read David's claims of integrity without falling into works-righteousness. Piper addresses this head-on: the psalmist's claims of blamelessness, uprightness, integrity, and righteousness are not legalism or pride. The psalmists "were justified by faith alone. But their faith 'worked through love.' It produced blamelessness and uprightness and integrity and righteousness. This was a work of the sanctifying Spirit of God." Imputed righteousness is the foundation, but not the summation. "Therefore, when you read in the Psalms that the psalmists offer up their blamelessness … don't over-spiritualize it. Don't treat it as perfectionism. Don't think of it as legalism. Don't demean it as a defective part of the 'old covenant.' Take it for what it is: a godly man, who knows he is a sinner, pardoned for God's name's sake, justified by grace, trusting God's mercy, depending on God's Spirit … and therefore walking in integrity and honesty and uprightness."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/can-anyone-really-be-blameless

### Baptist — Charles Spurgeon (Treasury of David)

Spurgeon holds the same tension but with a characteristically vivid edge. He insists David's appeal to integrity is valid only regarding specific false charges, not absolute sinlessness. "He had need have a clear case who dares to carry his suit into the King's Bench of heaven." For the whole of life, the only proper plea is "Enter not into judgment with thy servant." Spurgeon emphasizes that faith is the root of integrity, and that the psalm's confidence rests finally on covenant faithfulness, not human merit.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps026.php

### Pentecostal / Charismatic — David Guzik (Enduring Word)

Guzik reads Psalm 26 along similar lines to the traditional Reformed–evangelical consensus. He underscores that David "did not believe he was sinless or perfect" and that the washing of hands in innocence represents a clear conscience regarding specific accusations, not moral perfection. His emphasis is pastoral and applicational: choosing associations wisely, loving God's presence, and combining resolve with trust in God's mercy. He cites Boice repeatedly and applies the psalm to modern entertainment choices.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/

### Evangelical / "Bible Church" — Warren Wiersbe (Precept Austin)

Wiersbe frames Psalm 26 as "A Christian's Defense" against slander through four steps: (1) an honest examination (vv.1–3), (2) a holy separation (vv.4–5), (3) a happy celebration (vv.6–8), and (4) a humble determination (vv.9–12). He emphasises that "integrity means that your life is whole, that your heart is not divided" and links it to Jesus' teaching that no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24). "Character is a marvelous shield against the accusations of men."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/Integrity_a_whole_heart

### Older Anglican / Broad Church — Charles Ellicott

Ellicott notes the psalm's "priestly or Levitical" character (from vv.6–8), calling it "calm and regular, composed of twelve verses, each verse a distich." He connects the hand-washing and altar-procession to Temple ritual, noting Talmudic evidence for marching around the altar at the Feast of Tabernacles, while conceding there is no other direct reference to the custom in Jewish literature. His tone is descriptive and historical rather than hortatory.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm

---

## Points of Tension Among Traditions

**The claim of integrity (v.1, v.11).** All surveyed traditions agree David is not claiming sinless perfection. The differences are ones of emphasis:
- **Reformed (Piper):** These claims are the real fruit of sanctification, not imputed righteousness alone. Christians today should be able to say the same.
- **Baptist (Spurgeon/Gill):** The claim is limited to the specific false charge; David would never make this claim about his whole life.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Emphasises the pastoral dimension — a clear conscience before God combined with trust in mercy.
- **Wesleyan/Holiness (Wiersbe):** Emphasises integrity as "wholeness of character" and an undivided heart, which is the mark of sanctified living.
— Sources as noted above.

**"Go about Your altar" (v.6).** Ellicott raises the question of a ritual procession around the altar, attested in the Talmud for Tabernacles but otherwise unknown. Guzik notes Maclaren thought it referred figuratively to "a happy circle of worshippers," while Poole thought it meant many sacrifices circling the altar. No major doctrinal divide here, but a minor exegetical one.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/26.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-26/
